name: Social Facilitation
statement: People often perform simple or well-learned tasks better, but complex tasks worse, in the presence of others.
statementAccent: perform simple or well-learned tasks better
meaning: Social facilitation is the tendency for the mere presence of other people — as an audience or as co-actors — to affect individual task performance. The direction depends on task difficulty: easy or dominant responses tend to improve, while difficult or newly learned responses tend to worsen.
mechanism: Robert Zajonc’s 1965 drive theory proposed that the presence of others raises physiological arousal, which strengthens whatever response is dominant for a task. For simple, well-practised tasks the dominant response is usually correct, so performance improves; for complex or novel tasks the dominant response is often wrong, so performance suffers.

examples.text: In 1898 Norman Triplett had 40 children wind a fishing reel alone versus alongside another child; children wound faster when paired, which Triplett attributed to the presence of another contestant — a founding observation, though about half his participants showed no effect.

Zajonc tested cockroaches running simple versus complex mazes alone or with an audience of other roaches; presence sped up the simple straight-runway task but slowed the complex maze, supporting the drive-theory prediction across species.

A 2005 statistical reexamination by Michael Strube of Triplett’s 1898 data found the alone-versus-paired differences were small and not statistically significant, showing the founding result was weaker than textbooks portrayed.

whyItMatters: The theory underlies practical concerns such as test anxiety, stage fright, and workplace productivity — predicting when an audience or coworkers help versus hurt performance — and it remains a foundational finding in the history of experimental social psychology.
limits: Effects are often small, inconsistent across studies, and modern reanalysis suggests the classic 1898 result was statistically weak. Later refinements — evaluation apprehension, distraction-conflict theory — show arousal from mere presence is not the whole story.
misreadings: It is often oversimplified as "people always perform better when watched," ignoring the crucial, well-documented reversal for complex or unlearned tasks.
origin: First empirically observed by Norman Triplett in 1898; the drive-theory explanation was formalised by Robert Zajonc in his 1965 Science paper "Social Facilitation."

sources.text: Norman Triplett, Wikipedia. — his 1898 fishing-reel experiment, its interpretation, and Strube’s 2005 reanalysis.
Zajonc, R. B. (1965), "Social Facilitation," Science 149, 269-274 — the drive-theory mechanism and its 1965 origin.
